prompt: In cache-aside, who loads data into the cache on a miss?

options.text: The application
The cache, using a loader function
The database, through a trigger
Nobody; cache-aside only caches writes

explanation: In cache-aside the cache is passive; the application reads the database on a miss and stores the result. (b) describes read-through. (c) Databases don't push into the cache in this pattern. (d) Cache-aside is primarily a read pattern; writes just invalidate.

scenario: A service uses cache-aside with Redis. The Redis cluster becomes unreachable for ten minutes. The code treats any cache error as a miss.

options.text: All reads fail until Redis returns
Reads still succeed from the database, but slower, and the database takes the full read load
Reads return stale data from Redis's disk
Writes fail but reads are unaffected

explanation: Cache-aside falls back to the source of truth, so reads stay correct; the real danger is whether the database can absorb 100% of reads. (a) would only happen if cache errors weren't handled. (c) Unreachable means nothing is served from Redis at all. (d) Writes go to the database and only the delete fails, while reads are definitely affected in latency and load.

prompt: What is a practical advantage of a read-through cache library over hand-written cache-aside?

options.text: It removes the need for a database
Loading logic lives in one place, and concurrent misses for a key can be coalesced into one database read
It guarantees the cache is never stale
It makes writes faster

explanation: Read-through centralises the miss path and good libraries coalesce concurrent loads. (a) The database is still the source of truth. (c) Staleness still depends on invalidation and TTLs. (d) Read-through is about reads; write speed depends on the write strategy.

prompt: Under write-through, when is the client told the write succeeded?

options.text: As soon as the cache has the value
After both the cache and the database have the value
After the next read confirms it
After the TTL expires

explanation: Write-through is synchronous to both stores. (a) describes write-behind. (c) and (d) aren't part of any standard write strategy.

prompt: Which statements about write-through are true? (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: A read straight after a write is usually a hit with the new value
Each write pays the latency of both the cache and the database
It guarantees cache and database can never disagree
It can fill the cache with values nobody reads, so a TTL is still useful

explanation: (a) The written value is placed in the cache. (b) Both hops are synchronous. (d) Every write is cached, read or not. (c) is false: the two updates aren't atomic, so a crash between them or concurrent writers in different orders can leave them out of step.

prompt: How many acknowledged writes could be lost?
scenario: A write-behind cache takes 8,000 writes a second, spread evenly across 4 nodes, and flushes each node's dirty entries to the database every 3 seconds. One node crashes just before its flush.

options.text: About 2,000
About 6,000
About 24,000
None, because the writes were acknowledged

explanation: The node receives 8,000 ÷ 4 = 2,000 writes a second, and up to 3 seconds are unflushed: 6,000. (a) counts only one second. (c) counts all four nodes. (d) is the trap: under write-behind, acknowledged means 'in the cache', not 'durable'.

prompt: Which data is the safest fit for write-behind?
scenario: A social app is considering write-behind for four kinds of writes: new user sign-ups, payment captures, per-post view counters, and direct messages.

options.text: New user sign-ups
Payment captures
Per-post view counters
Direct messages

explanation: View counters are high-rate, benefit from batching, and losing a few seconds of increments is harmless. (a) A lost sign-up means a user who was told their account exists has none. (b) Losing a captured payment is a financial error. (d) Users notice and care about lost messages.

prompt: Which write strategy fits this data best?
scenario: An audit service writes 30,000 audit events a second. Fewer than 1% are ever read, usually weeks later during an investigation. The service also caches hot user records in the same Redis cluster.

options.text: Write-through, so every event is in the cache
Write-behind, to make the writes faster
Write-around: write events to the database only and let rare reads fill the cache
Cache every event with no TTL

explanation: Write-around keeps rarely read data out of the cache, so it doesn't evict the hot user records. (a) would flood the cache with 30,000 entries a second that are almost never read. (b) risks losing audit events, which defeats their purpose. (d) is (a) made worse: the cache fills and evicts everything useful.

prompt: Why is 'update the database, then delete the cache key' called write-around?

options.text: The write goes around the cache to the database, and the cache refills only on a later read
The write goes to the cache and around the database
Writes go around in a ring of cache nodes
The cache writes to the database on a timer

explanation: The cache isn't written; the database is, and a later miss reloads. (b) is closer to write-behind. (c) confuses this with consistent hashing. (d) describes write-behind flushing.

prompt: Which design is the best starting point?
scenario: You're adding a cache for product pages: 50,000 reads a second, about 20 product edits a minute, edits by staff who don't mind a few seconds' delay, and a database that can handle about 10,000 reads a second.

options.text: Cache-aside reads, update the database then delete the key on edits, plus a TTL
Write-behind for product edits
No cache; scale the database instead
Write-through with no TTL

explanation: A hugely read-heavy workload with rare edits that tolerate slight delay is the textbook case for cache-aside with delete on write and a TTL safety net. (b) risks losing edits to save time nobody needs saved. (c) The database is five times too small for the read load. (d) Write-through without a TTL lets any missed update or race persist forever.

prompt: Which strategy carries a durability risk from the cache itself?

options.text: Cache-aside
Write-through
Write-around
Write-behind

explanation: Only write-behind acknowledges writes before the database has them. (a) and (c) write the database directly. (b) writes the database synchronously before acknowledging.
